title: Physical Assessment in Metabolic and Endocrine Disorders
path: Management of Clients with Problems of the Metabolic and Endocrine System

headings.title: Introduction to Endocrine Physical Assessment
headings.content: Physical assessment of the endocrine and metabolic systems is a foundational competency for nursing students in Nigeria, bridging the gap between pathophysiology and holistic patient care. Hormones regulate virtually every physiological process in the human body, including growth, metabolism, fluid balance, and response to stress. When these chemical messengers are secreted in excess or deficiency, distinct clinical manifestations appear across various body systems. Conducting a systematic physical examination allows the nurse to detect early signs of disorders such as diabetes mellitus, thyroid dysfunctions, and adrenal abnormalities before severe complications arise. Unlike systems with localized anatomical structures, the endocrine system comprises glands scattered throughout the body, from the hypothalamus and pituitary in the head to the thyroid in the neck, and the adrenals and pancreas in the abdomen. Therefore, the nursing assessment must be comprehensive, methodical, and observant of subtle changes in appearance, behavior, and physiological parameters. By integrating a thorough health history with a targeted physical exam, student nurses can identify critical cues, prioritize nursing diagnoses, and collaborate effectively with the multidisciplinary healthcare team to manage metabolic crises. Mastering this assessment technique ensures safer clinical practice and aligns with regional healthcare priorities focused on chronic non-communicable disease management.

headings.title: Preparation and General Inspection of the Client
headings.content: Preparation and general inspection are the critical first steps in performing an accurate metabolic and endocrine physical assessment. Before touching the client, the nurse must ensure a comfortable, well-lit environment and establish a trusting nurse-client relationship to alleviate anxiety, which can artificially alter vital signs and physiological responses. General inspection begins the moment the nurse first encounters the client, observing overall appearance, body habitus, posture, and facial expressions. The nurse should note nutritional status, symmetry, and any obvious signs of distress or abnormal fat distribution, such as the truncal obesity, buffalo hump, and moon face characteristic of Cushing's syndrome, or the profound cachexia seen in uncontrolled type 1 diabetes or advanced thyrotoxicosis. Evaluating the client's level of consciousness, mood, and cognitive function is equally vital, as metabolic shifts frequently induce lethargy, irritability, anxiety, or confusion. Attention should also be paid to speech patterns and voice tone, noting whether the speech is slow and slurred, which might suggest hypothyroidism, or rapid and pressured, which could indicate hyperthyroidism. Preparing the client properly involves explaining each step of the exam to gain cooperation and reduce fear, thereby facilitating a more reliable and clinically useful physical evaluation.

headings.title: Assessment of the Skin, Hair, and Nails
headings.content: Assessment of the skin, hair, and nails provides invaluable diagnostic clues regarding underlying metabolic and endocrine function. Hormones exert profound trophic effects on integumentary structures, meaning alterations in texture, moisture, pigmentation, and distribution often mirror internal endocrine imbalances. When inspecting the skin, the nurse should assess for temperature, moisture, texture, turgor, and lesions. For instance, warm, smooth, and excessively moist skin is frequently associated with hyperthyroidism, whereas cool, dry, rough, and thickened skin suggests hypothyroidism. Skin pigmentation changes must also be noted; generalized hyperpigmentation, particularly in sun-exposed areas and palmar creases, is a classic hallmark of Addison's disease due to elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels stimulating melanocytes. Hair distribution should be evaluated for thinning, alopecia, or hirsutism, which is abnormal female hair growth on the face and trunk often linked to polycystic ovary syndrome or adrenal tumors. Nail examination may reveal brittle, thin, or ridged nails associated with poor nutritional status or thyroid disorders. Palpating skin turgor helps evaluate hydration status, which is especially critical in clients experiencing diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state, where severe dehydration causes tenting and dry mucous membranes.

headings.title: Examination of the Head, Eyes, and Neck
headings.content: Examination of the head, eyes, and neck focuses heavily on evaluating the structures most visibly impacted by thyroid and pituitary disorders. Beginning with the head and face, the nurse inspects facial symmetry, jaw size, and expression. Coarse facial features, macroglossia, and periorbital edema are common in severe hypothyroidism (myxedema), whereas prominent facial bone growth and enlarged jaw (prognathism) indicate acromegaly resulting from excess growth hormone. Eye assessment is crucial; the nurse must inspect for exophthalmos, a forward protrusion of the eyeballs characteristic of Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism), along with lid lag and infrequent blinking. Visual acuity and extraocular movements should also be checked, as pituitary tumors can compress the optic chiasm, causing visual field defects like bitemporal hemianopsia. The neck examination centers primarily on the thyroid gland. The nurse inspects the anterior neck for visible swelling or asymmetry while the client swallows a sip of water, which causes the thyroid to rise. Palpation of the thyroid can be performed using either an anterior or posterior approach. The nurse gently feels for the thyroid lobes and isthmus, assessing for overall size, symmetry, contour, and the presence of nodules, tenderness, or thrills. If an enlarged thyroid (goiter) is palpated, the nurse should auscultate the gland with the bell of the stethoscope to detect bruits, which indicate hypervascularity associated with hyperthyroidism.

headings.title: Evaluation of the Cardiovascular and Vital Signs
headings.content: Evaluation of the cardiovascular system and vital signs provides essential data on how endocrine imbalances affect hemodynamic stability and metabolic rate. Thyroid hormones, catecholamines, and insulin directly influence heart rate, myocardial contractility, blood pressure, and vascular tone. When measuring vital signs, the nurse must systematically assess temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory rate. Tachycardia, wide pulse pressure, and systolic hypertension are frequent manifestations of hyperthyroidism due to heightened sympathetic nervous system activity and increased metabolic demand. Conversely, bradycardia, narrow pulse pressure, and hypotension can signal hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency (Addisonian crisis). Orthostatic vital signs should be checked if fluid volume depletion or adrenal crisis is suspected, noting a significant drop in blood pressure and rise in heart rate when moving from a lying to a standing position. Cardiovascular auscultation involves listening for heart sounds, rhythm irregularities, and murmurs. Arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation are commonly triggered by thyrotoxicosis and require careful documentation. Additionally, respiratory patterns should be evaluated; Kussmaul respirations—deep, rapid, and labored breathing—are a critical sign of respiratory compensation in severe metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), demanding immediate emergency nursing intervention.

headings.title: Abdominal and Musculoskeletal Assessment
headings.content: Abdominal and musculoskeletal assessment in endocrine and metabolic disorders uncovers critical systemic manifestations involving visceral fat deposition, organomegaly, and bone mineralization. During abdominal inspection, the nurse observes contour and symmetry, noting central adiposity, striae, and abdominal distension. Purple or violaceous abdominal striae are highly indicative of excess cortisol production in Cushing's syndrome, contrasting with the normal pink or silvery striae associated with weight gain or pregnancy. Palpation of the abdomen may reveal hepatomegaly or splenomegaly, which can occur in lipid metabolism disorders or advanced endocrine malignancies. Auscultation for bowel sounds is performed to assess gastrointestinal motility, which is slowed in hypothyroidism (leading to severe constipation and ileus) and accelerated in hyperthyroidism (leading to frequent loose stools). Musculoskeletal assessment focuses on muscle strength, tone, skeletal structure, and reflexes. Endocrine disorders frequently affect the musculoskeletal system; for example, hyperparathyroidism can cause bone demineralization, pathological fractures, and bone pain due to excessive parathyroid hormone pulling calcium from the bones. Proximal muscle weakness is a classic feature of Cushing's syndrome and hyperthyroidism, making it difficult for the client to rise from a squatting position or climb stairs without assistance. Assessing gait, posture, and joint stability helps the nurse gauge the overall functional impact of the metabolic disorder on the client's daily life.

headings.title: Neurological and Reflex Examination
headings.content: Neurological and reflex examination is essential because metabolic and endocrine imbalances profoundly impact central and peripheral nervous system function. The nurse evaluates mental status, sensory function, cranial nerves, and deep tendon reflexes. Neurological manifestations can range from subtle anxiety and tremors to life-threatening comas. Fine tremors of the outstretched fingers are commonly observed in clients with hyperthyroidism due to nervous system hyperexcitability. Conversely, delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes—particularly the Achilles tendon reflex (Worster-Drought reflex)—is a classic, highly specific indicator of hypothyroidism. Electrolyte disturbances secondary to endocrine dysfunction, such as severe hyponatremia in Addison's disease or syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), can precipitate confusion, lethargy, seizures, or coma. Testing for neuromuscular irritability is crucial in suspected hypocalcemia resulting from hypoparathyroidism or accidental parathyroid gland removal during thyroid surgery. The nurse tests for Chvostek's sign by tapping the facial nerve just anterior to the earlobe, observing for facial twitching, and Trousseau's sign by inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for three minutes, watching for carpal spasm. Positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs indicate tetany and latent hypocalcemia, requiring immediate intervention to prevent laryngospasm and seizures.

headings.title: Documentation and Specialized Diagnostic Correlation
headings.content: Documentation and specialized diagnostic correlation complete the nursing assessment process, ensuring continuity of care and effective interprofessional communication. Accurate and objective documentation of physical assessment findings provides a baseline to evaluate therapeutic interventions and disease progression over time. The nurse must record all abnormal findings clearly, using precise medical terminology rather than vague descriptions. For example, rather than writing 'neck looks swollen,' the nurse should document 'visible anterior neck enlargement measuring approximately 5 cm in the thyroid region, moving upward on deglutition, with a palpable thrill.' Physical assessment data must never be interpreted in isolation; instead, it must be correlated with specialized diagnostic investigations. Blood glucose monitoring, thyroid function tests (TSH, free T3, free T4), serum electrolytes, cortisol levels, and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) provide objective laboratory confirmation of physical findings. Imaging studies such as thyroid ultrasounds, CT scans of the adrenals or pituitary, and bone density scans further clarify structural abnormalities. For nursing students in Nigeria, mastering this correlation reinforces clinical reasoning, enabling them to anticipate medical orders, educate clients on diagnostic preparations, and recognize critical laboratory values that require immediate escalation to the attending physician.
